function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL and retrieves data as specified by the parameters. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. It is expected to be a well-formed HTTP or HTTPS URL.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: A dictionary of HTTP headers to send with the request. Each key-value pair represents a header name and its value.

timeout.description: The number of seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, as a float, or a (connect_timeout, read_timeout) tuple. This is a float type value.

lat.description: Latitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

lon.description: Longitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters to append to the URL for the GET request.

allow_redirects.description: Determines if HTTP redirections (301, 302, etc.) should be followed.

auth.description: A tuple representing the user credentials for HTTP authentication, typically in the form of (username, password).

cert.description: Path to an SSL certificate file to verify the peer, or a tuple of (certificate file, key file).

cookies.description: A dictionary of cookies to send with the request. The key is the cookie name and the value is the cookie value.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: A dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy.

stream.description: If True, the response content will not be downloaded immediately but streamed.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not, or a path to a CA bundle if verification is needed.

message.content:
There’s no single answer that everyone agrees on—greatness in basketball depends on what you’re looking at (statistics, championships, influence, longevity, versatility). Here are some of the most frequently cited candidates:

| Player | Era | Key Achievements |
|--------|-----|------------------|
| **Michael Jordan** | ’80s‑’90s | 6 NBA titles, 5 MVP awards, 10 scoring titles, 14 All‑Star selections, two Olympic gold medals (1984 & 1992), dominant clutch performances (“Flu Game,” “Last Shot”). Often called the benchmark for greatness because he combined individual brilliance with championship success. |
| **LeBron James** | Early 2000s–present | 4 NBA titles, 4 MVP awards, 19 All‑Stars so far, all‑time leader in points among active players, versatile playmaking, sustained excellence across multiple teams (Cleveland, Miami, Los Angeles, Brooklyn). His career spans over two decades while still performing at elite levels. |
| **Kareem Abdul‑Jabbar** | ’70s‑’80s | Most‑scored player in NBA history, six MVP awards (the record), six championships, legendary skyhook shot, long‑term consistency from rookie year through his late thirties. He dominated both offense and defense throughout his career. |
| **Bill Russell** | ’50s‑’60s | Five consecutive NBA championships with Boston Celtics, five Finals MVPs, known for defensive mastery and leadership. While stats were modest compared to modern numbers, his impact on team success was huge. |
| **Magic Johnson** | ’80s | Three MVP awards, three Defensive Player of the Year honors, eight All‑NBA First Team selections, led Lakers to five championships, revolutionized point‑forward role. |

### Why it stays debated

1. **Different eras:** Rules, pace, athleticism, and competition level vary widely between the ‘40s and today. Comparing raw statistics across time requires adjustments (pace, era‑adjusted metrics).

2. **Championship vs. Individual skill:** Some argue championships trump everything else (e.g., Jordan); others emphasize statistical dominance and overall talent (e.g., LeBron, Kareem).

3. **Longevity and health:** Players who maintain high performance into their mid‑30s (like LeBron) often get extra credit versus those whose prime lasted only a few years.

4. **Impact beyond the court:** Cultural influence, marketability, philanthropy also factor into how people view legacy.

In short, many would say *“It depends.”* For pure title count and iconic moments, Jordan tops the list. For consistent, multi‑position excellence spanning decades, LeBron has strong claims. Historically, Russell and Kareem set standards that remain unmatched. Ultimately, each candidate brings unique strengths that shape why they might be deemed the greatest.
